reasoning:
Both outputs satisfy all four expectations, but B answers the question that was asked and A answers a larger one. The user said 'it writes migrations without a rollback step' and asked how to make a correction stick. B's spine is exactly that: storage/durability/enforcement diagnosis, then a fenced rule block under a heading that literally reads 'The rule block - paste this' at 22% of the document, then four candidate homes ranked by the single criterion 'whether it's actually loaded at the moment a migration is being written', then sequencing and a ten-minute version. On the 30-second skim test the grader flagged, B hands over something pasteable; A (406 lines) leads with a five-row assumptions table and a mandatory 'Step 1 - Reproduce it before you fix it (20 minutes)' before its template appears at line 119. A's reproduce-first argument is genuinely sharp - if Claude writes bad rollbacks rather than no rollbacks, a required slot manufactures confident garbage that now passes review - but the user already stated the failure is omission, and A concedes this in its own stress test ('you described the rollback as absent rather than empty'). A also repeats itself: 'grep is not proof' appears in Tier 2, Common Mistakes, and the Stress Test; 'don't add unless' appears twice. That extra material is partly load-bearing and partly padding.

On durability of the artifact itself, B wins on design. B's DB-001 is self-contained - Rule, Precedent, Self-check travel together in the one file that is always loaded - and the self-check is deliberately not answerable by feeling ('Count the migration files added or modified. Count the ones whose round-trip you just ran clean. The two numbers match, or the change isn't done'). A's always-loaded text is only four lines with no self-check and no evidence; the durable parts are outsourced to a template file and a hook. B also gives the better check on the merits: up->down->up against a scratch database proves the down works, where A's grep only proves a section exists (A says so honestly). B's vocabulary argument - use 'down' not 'rollback step', because 'down' is already a token in the model's priors and a phrase can be satisfied by a comment that says rollback - is the most specific mechanism in either document, and expectation 3 (why bare imperatives decay) is where B is strongest: 'An assertion is argued with. Evidence is only disproven,' plus the observation that a correction delivered after the migration is written is a repair, not an instruction.

I ran the shipped code. A is 4/4 clean: its hook accepts its own _TEMPLATE.sql (exit 0), rejects a migration with no rollback (exit 2), handles Alembic 'def downgrade', ignores non-migration paths, and its baseline git ls-files loop correctly flagged 1 of 3 fixtures. A's disclosed near-miss is real and admirable - the pattern needs the '#*' branch to match '-- ## ROLLBACK', and without it the checker would have rejected every file its own template produces - and A ships a self-test so the checker cannot rot into a meaningless green light. That is the best verification hygiene in either document and it is why the margin here is moderate rather than wide.

B's code is 2/3. Its four round-trip commands are all correct, and its zsh claim checks out (unquoted --include=*.jsonl errors 'no matches found' in zsh). Its CI gate correctly passes a good migration and a file marked 'irreversible:' and correctly fails an empty 'def downgrade(): pass' and a file with no down - but it false-positives on a valid migration whose *upgrade* is 'pass', because '^\s*pass\s*$' is file-scoped rather than scoped to the downgrade body. That fails closed (noisy, not silent), which is the safer direction. The real defect is B's precedent-extraction snippet: Claude Code transcripts carry user text at message.content, not top-level content, so d.get('content') returns None for every line. Run verbatim against the densest matching project directory it printed '2026-09-16T06:08:06.067Z None' for all 28 user lines - a silent failure, in the document that lectures about checks 'satisfiable by judgment' being decorative, sitting directly under a confident 'Verified on your machine just now' parenthetical that lends it unearned credibility. (That verification claim itself has drifted but is not fabricated: the count is now 116, not 92.) This is a genuine ding, but it is peripheral - it is a convenience for filling a slot, not the rule, the round-trip, or the placement analysis, all of which stand.

On honesty about evidence, the tiebreaker the grader raised, B is the clearer case. It leaves <dates> and '<paste your actual words here>' blank and defends the blank: 'A precedent invented at the desk is a stale line wearing armour... If you can't source it, leave the rule bare rather than dress it in a story.' It then grades its own precedent ('strong on recurrence, weak on cost - no production rollback has yet failed') and names the evidence that would retire it. A never faces this test but shows comparable discipline: disclosing its own regex bug and insisting on 'the weaker true thing: has a rollback section, not rollback tested.' Both are honest; neither fabricates. Net: A is the better-engineered checker, B is the better answer to the question, and on a prompt this specific the answer wins.
